Question: Elmo makes \(N\) sandwiches for a fundraiser. For each sandwich he uses \(B\) globs of peanut butter at \(4\)¢ per glob and \(J\) blobs of jam at \(5\)¢ per blob. The cost of the peanut butter and jam to make all the sandwiches is \(\$2.53.\) Assume that \(B,\) \(J,\) and \(N\) are positive integers with \(N \gt 1.\) What is the cost of the jam Elmo uses to make the sandwiches?
Solution:
Method 1: Method 1: Factor the total cost

Work in cents so that all costs are integers. Each sandwich costs \(4B+5J\) cents, so
\[
N(4B+5J)=253.
\]
Because both ingredients are used, \(4B+5J\ge9\). Hence \(2\le N\le28\), and \(N\) must divide \(253\). The factorization \(253=11\cdot23\), with both factors prime, shows that only \(N=11\) and \(N=23\) remain.

If \(N=23\), each sandwich costs \(11\) cents. Positivity forces \(J=1\), leaving \(6\) cents for peanut butter. This is impossible because peanut butter costs a multiple of \(4\) cents.

If \(N=11\), each sandwich costs \(23\) cents. Since at least \(4\) cents must be spent on peanut butter, \(J\) can only be \(1,2,3\). These choices leave \(18,13,8\) cents, respectively, for peanut butter. Only \(8\) is divisible by \(4\), so \(J=3\) and \(B=2\).

These cases exhaust all possible sandwich counts and ingredient amounts. The jam therefore costs
\[
5NJ=5\cdot11\cdot3=165\text{ cents}=\$1.65.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\$1.65}\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

Method 2: Method 2: Use the choices and common divisors

The total number of peanut-butter globs is \(NB\), and the total number of jam blobs is \(NJ\). Thus the number \(N>1\) of sandwiches must divide both ingredient counts.

For each proposed jam cost, divide that cost in cents by \(5\) to find the jam count. Subtract the jam cost from \(253\), then divide by \(4\) to find the peanut-butter count. Writing each pair as \((\text{jam count},\text{peanut-butter count})\), the five choices give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{A}&:(21,37),\\
\mathrm{B}&:(25,32),\\
\mathrm{C}&:(29,27),\\
\mathrm{D}&:(33,22),\\
\mathrm{E}&:(37,17).
\end{aligned}
\]
The greatest common divisors of these pairs are, respectively, \(1,1,1,11,1\). Therefore only choice \(\mathrm{D}\) allows a common divisor \(N>1\).

It is also feasible: take \(N=11\), \(J=3\), and \(B=2\). Then
\[
11(4\cdot2+5\cdot3)=253,
\]
and the jam costs \(5\cdot11\cdot3=165\) cents. The answer is \(\boxed{\$1.65}\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
